cues.text: Let us turn now to the second part of this chapter: digital-first culture and leadership.
Before any technology is bought or any process is redesigned, an organisation has to ask a simple question: how do people here actually behave, and what do they believe is normal?
That is what culture is.
A digital-first culture is one in which people naturally think, decide and work in ways that make good use of digital tools, data and new ideas.
It is not a gadget.
It is a set of habits and values.
The source lists a group of supporting attributes.

They are agility, customer-centricity, experimentation, psychological safety, continuous learning, data-informed decisions, cross-functional collaboration, openness, adaptability and ethical accountability.
Let us take them in that order.
Agility is the ability to respond quickly and sensibly when conditions change.
Customer-centricity means the customer's needs and experience guide what the organisation does.
Experimentation means testing ideas on a small scale to learn what works.
Psychological safety means people feel able to speak up without fear of humiliation; we will return to this shortly.
Continuous learning means skills and knowledge are refreshed all the time, not only at a training event.
Data-informed decisions means evidence shapes choices, rather than habit or the loudest voice.
Cross-functional collaboration means people from different departments work together towards shared outcomes.
Openness means information and ideas are shared willingly.
Adaptability means the organisation can adjust its ways of working.
And ethical accountability means people take responsibility for acting properly as they use data and technology.
Now look at the table that follows, which you can see in the accompanying visual.
It has two columns.
The left column is headed "Analogue-oriented habit", and the right column is headed "Digital-first alternative".
Each row pairs an old habit with its replacement.

Row one: rigid departmental handoffs, where work is passed over a wall from one department to the next, is replaced by cross-functional ownership, where a mixed group shares responsibility for the result.
Row two: decisions only by hierarchy, where everything waits for someone senior, is replaced by delegated decisions within guardrails.
Notice the phrase "within guardrails".
Staff are trusted to decide, but inside agreed limits.
Row three: annual-only feedback, where you learn how you did once a year, is replaced by frequent measurement and iteration, meaning you measure often and improve in repeated cycles.
Row four: a paper or manual default is replaced by appropriate integrated digital workflows.
The word "appropriate" matters.
The aim is not to digitise everything blindly, but to use digital workflows that fit the task and connect with one another.
Row five: fear of failure is replaced by safe-to-fail experiments and learning.
Experiments are designed so that if they fail, the damage is small and the lesson is kept.
Row six: knowledge silos, where information stays locked inside one team, is replaced by transparent information and shared practices.
Next, the building blocks.

The source names digital vision, leadership commitment, customer focus, data literacy, digital skills, agile workflows, accessible tools, collaboration, flexible work where feasible, and continuous improvement.
Digital vision tells people where the organisation is heading.
Leadership commitment shows that the vision is serious.
Data literacy is the ability to read, question and use data.
Digital skills are the practical abilities to work with digital tools.
Agile workflows organise work in short, adaptable cycles.
Flexible work is included only where feasible, which is a qualification worth keeping.
The source adds that digital communication tools such as Teams, Slack and Trello can support coordination.
But it gives a clear warning: tools cannot remove conflicting incentives by themselves.
If one department is rewarded for hoarding information, a shared messaging app will not change that.
The incentives must change too.
This brings us to leadership.
According to the source, leaders model the desired behaviour, sponsor change, provide resources, build capabilities, empower teams and align rewards.
Modelling means they do what they ask others to do.
Sponsoring means they visibly back the change.
Providing resources means giving time, budget and tools.
Building capabilities means developing people's skills.
Empowering means giving teams real authority.
Aligning rewards means making sure incentives support the new behaviour.
On psychological safety, the source is precise.
It means people can raise concerns and learn without humiliation.
It does not mean an absence of accountability.
People are still answerable for their work; they are simply not punished for honesty.
As for rewards, the source says to reward transparent issue reporting, quality, customer outcomes and collaborative improvement, rather than raw activity counts.
Counting how many emails were sent or hours were logged tells you little.
Rewarding outcomes and openness encourages the right behaviour.
Now, how do we actually change a culture?
The source offers Kotter's eight-step change model.
Step one is urgency: help people see why change is needed now.
Step two is a guiding coalition: assemble a group with the influence to lead it.
Step three is vision: describe clearly what the future looks like.
Step four is communication and mobilisation: share the vision widely and get people moving.
Step five is removing barriers: clear away obstacles such as outdated rules or missing skills.
Step six is short-term wins: show early, visible successes.
Step seven is sustaining acceleration: keep the momentum going rather than declaring victory too early.
Step eight is anchoring change: make the new ways part of everyday practice.
The source stresses that cultural transformation requires consistent reinforcement.
One announcement is never enough.
It suggests using change champions, mentoring, training and feedback.
Change champions are respected colleagues who help their peers adopt the new ways.
It also says to adapt leadership communication to stakeholders without stereotyping.
Different groups may need different messages, but you must not assume things about people because of their age, role or background.
Finally, the Nigerian examples.
The teaching materials mention UBA, the United Bank for Africa, for its leadership and digital banking, and Andela for its emphasis on digital skills.
The source is careful about the lesson here.
It is the importance of visible leadership and capability building.
It is not an assumption that every practice transfers unchanged to another organisation.
What worked in one setting must be adapted, not simply copied.
